title: The Polis
objective: After this level you can explain what a Greek city-state was.
summary: A polis was an independent town plus its countryside; there were over a thousand, most of them small, and the word lives on in “politics”.

cards.headline: Ancient Greece had no capital city. It had more than a thousand cities.
cards.body: No single king, no one government, no national flag. So what exactly was a Greek city, and why were there so many?

cards.headline: A town with its farms attached
cards.body: The Greek word is polis, usually translated “city-state”. A polis was a town plus the countryside for some miles around, villages and all. Picture your town, the farms beyond it, and a line where the next town’s fields begin. Now give that town its own government. Each polis was independent of its neighbors, and the Greek city-states never formed a permanent union.

mascot.line: Keep this picture: a town, its fields and its own government. That’s a polis.

cards.headline: Small by design
cards.body: Scholars have catalogued 1,035 Greek city-states, out of some 1,500 in all. Most were tiny by our standards: several hundred to a couple of thousand people, closer to a big school than a big city. The island of Lesbos alone held five of them. Imagine five countries sharing one island, each sure it was the best.

cards.headline: Why so many?
cards.body: Remember Level 2? Mountains made travel hard, so communities in separate valleys grew up apart and independently. The polis emerged around 750 BCE and stayed the main way Greeks organized themselves until the Roman Empire. It still lives in your vocabulary: politics comes from Greek politikos, “of citizens”, from polis. Talk politics and you’re talking city-state business.

cards.headline: The polis: explained
learned: A polis was a town plus its countryside
Each was independent; there was no permanent union

questions.prompt: Besides its town, what did an ancient Greek polis include?

options.label: Only the walled streets of the town
options.rationale: It took in the farmland too.

options.label: The surrounding countryside and its villages
Every Greek-speaking region
options.rationale: Each polis was one town and its land.

questions.explanation: A polis was a town plus the countryside for some miles around, villages and all.

questions.prompt: Why do historians translate polis as “city-state” rather than just “city”?

options.label: Each polis was ruled from Athens
Most poleis held millions of people
options.rationale: Most had a few thousand at most.

options.label: Each polis was an independent state with its own government
The poleis were provinces of one Greek kingdom

questions.explanation: A polis governed itself, independent of its neighbors, like a tiny country.

questions.prompt: How did the mountains of Level 2 help produce so many separate Greek city-states?

options.label: Mountain kings forced towns to split apart
options.rationale: Geography, not kings, kept them apart.

options.label: Rome divided the land into city-states
options.rationale: The polis came long before Roman rule.

options.label: Communities in separate valleys grew up apart

questions.explanation: Mountains made overland travel hard, so valley communities grew up independently.
